---
title: "G4: Amateur Radio Practices"
---

This section covers the practical side of operating an amateur radio station: how to adjust a transceiver's controls for optimal signal quality, how to use test equipment, how to ground your station safely, and how to operate from a vehicle or alternative power source. The underlying physics and engineering behind each practice are explained in enough depth to make the rules genuinely intelligible rather than memorized.

---

## Receiver Controls and Signal Processing

A modern HF transceiver (a device that combines both a transmitter and a receiver in one unit — "transceiver" = transmitter + receiver) contains an extensive set of adjustable controls for the receiver section. Understanding what each one does requires a brief picture of how a receiver works.

An HF receiver takes a tiny RF (radio frequency) voltage from the antenna — often just microvolts, i.e., millionths of a volt — and ultimately produces audible audio at the speaker. The signal passes through several stages: a *front-end* preamplifier (which boosts the weak antenna signal), one or more *mixing* stages (which shift the signal down from the received frequency to a fixed *intermediate frequency* or IF), an *IF filter* (which selects only the desired signal bandwidth and rejects everything else), a *detector* (which extracts the audio from the IF signal), and finally an *audio amplifier*. Interference and noise can enter at any stage, which is why there are controls targeting each different type of problem.

### Notch Filter

A **notch filter** is a very narrow band-reject filter — it removes a tiny slice of frequency from the received audio while passing everything else. Specifically, it is used to eliminate a single interfering *carrier*: an unmodulated continuous-wave tone or a "heterodyne whistle" that sits inside the passband of the desired signal. The interfering carrier appears in the received audio as a steady, annoying tone. The notch filter "notches out" that one frequency without affecting the surrounding voice or data signal. Modern transceivers implement this in DSP (Digital Signal Processing), which allows the notch to track a drifting interferer automatically.

The notch filter does *not* affect impulsive noise, strong signal overload, or interference from other SSB (Single Sideband — a voice mode) signals. It is specifically a narrow-tone remover.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A01: What is the purpose of the notch filter found on many HF transceivers?

- A) To restrict the transmitter voice bandwidth
- **B) To reduce interference from carriers in the receiver passband**
- C) To eliminate receiver interference from impulse noise sources
- D) To remove interfering splatter generated by signals on adjacent frequencies
:::

### Reverse Sideband for CW

CW (Continuous Wave — Morse code) signals appear as audio tones in an SSB receiver, because the SSB receiver converts an on-off RF signal at some offset frequency into an on-off audio tone. When receiving CW on USB (Upper Sideband), a CW signal slightly below the receiver's dial frequency falls outside the filter passband, but a signal slightly above falls inside.

Switching the receiver to the "opposite" or reverse sideband (e.g., switching from USB to LSB while keeping the same dial frequency) effectively mirrors the filter passband around the carrier frequency. This moves the CW tone to the opposite side of the passband. If an interfering CW signal was just outside the filter edge and causing a problem, this mirror operation may shift it clearly outside the new passband, reducing or eliminating the interference. It is a simple, zero-cost trick that exploits the symmetry of the filter.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A02: What is the benefit of using the opposite or "reverse" sideband when receiving CW?

- A) Interference from impulse noise will be eliminated
- B) More stations can be accommodated within a given signal passband
- **C) It may be possible to reduce or eliminate interference from other signals**
- D) Accidental out-of-band operation can be prevented
:::

### Noise Blanker

A **noise blanker** targets impulsive noise: brief, very strong noise spikes from automotive ignition systems, power-line arc dischargers, electric fences, or fluorescent light starters. These sources produce pulses that are loud and short — they dominate the received audio as sharp clicks or buzzing.

The noise blanker works by monitoring the received signal for very high-amplitude, very short-duration pulses. When it detects such a pulse, it briefly *reduces the receiver's gain* (sensitivity) for the duration of that pulse — essentially "blanking" the input. Because the pulse is so short (microseconds), the loss of signal during the blank is imperceptible; the desired signal is smeared out over time and the blank interval is too short to register as a gap. The result: the click is eliminated without audibly affecting the desired signal.

The noise blanker detects pulses by their *amplitude envelope* — not by their audio content. This is why it does not work on broadband noise (atmospheric static), which lacks discrete high-amplitude spikes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A03: How does a noise blanker work?

- A) By temporarily increasing received bandwidth
- B) By redirecting noise pulses into a filter capacitor
- **C) By reducing receiver gain during a noise pulse**
- D) By clipping noise peaks
:::

### DSP Noise Reduction

**DSP noise reduction** is a different approach to noise. Where the noise blanker targets discrete spikes, DSP noise reduction targets broadband white noise — the hiss that underlies all received signals. Modern transceivers use DSP algorithms (often adaptive filters or spectral subtraction) that attempt to model the noise spectrum and subtract it from the received audio, leaving only the signal.

The catch: increasing noise reduction too aggressively causes artifacts. The algorithm begins to "eat into" the signal itself, misclassifying signal energy as noise. The result: voices become robotic and synthetic-sounding, and fine detail in weak signals is lost. A moderate noise reduction setting significantly improves signal intelligibility on a noisy path; a maximum setting often makes weak signals *less* intelligible because of the distortion introduced.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A07: What happens as a receiver's noise reduction control level is increased?

- **A) Received signals may become distorted**
- B) Received frequency may become unstable
- C) CW signals may become severely attenuated
- D) Received frequency may shift several kHz
:::

### Dual VFO

A **VFO** (Variable Frequency Oscillator) is the circuit that sets the receiver's (and transmitter's) operating frequency. Most modern transceivers contain two independent VFOs, labeled VFO-A and VFO-B. This dual-VFO feature has several practical uses:

- **Split operation**: transmit on one frequency (using one VFO) and receive on a different frequency (using the other VFO). This is commonly used when working rare DX (long-distance) stations that specify a transmit frequency and a separate listening range.
- **Frequency comparison**: quickly toggle between two frequencies to compare conditions.
- **Frequency scratch pad**: set VFO-B to a frequency of interest while continuing to work on VFO-A.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A12: Which of the following is a common use of the dual-VFO feature on a transceiver?

- A) To allow transmitting on two frequencies at once
- B) To permit full duplex operation -- that is, transmitting and receiving at the same time
- **C) To transmit on one frequency and listen on another**
- D) To improve frequency accuracy by allowing variable frequency output (VFO) operation
:::

### Receive Attenuator

A **receive attenuator** (also called an "attenuator" or "pad") is a resistive network that deliberately reduces the signal level reaching the receiver's front-end amplifier. This sounds counterproductive — why reduce signal? — but it solves a specific problem: *receiver overload*.

When a very strong signal (for example, from a nearby powerful transmitter or a local broadcast station) enters the receiver's preamplifier, it can drive that amplifier beyond its linear operating range. A non-linear amplifier generates *intermodulation products* — spurious signals at sum and difference frequencies of the strong input signals. These appear as phantom stations, noise, and interference across many frequencies. Inserting 10–20 dB of attenuation before the front end reduces all signal levels, keeping the preamplifier in its linear range. The desired weak signal drops in level, but so does the interfering strong signal, and the overall reception quality improves because the non-linear distortion is eliminated.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A13: What is the purpose of using a receive attenuator?

- **A) To prevent receiver overload from strong incoming signals**
- B) To reduce the transmitter power when driving a linear amplifier
- C) To reduce power consumption when operating from batteries
- D) To reduce excessive audio level on strong signals
:::

## Transmitter Controls — ALC, Drive, and Keying

### ALC: Automatic Level Control

**ALC** (Automatic Level Control) is a feedback control loop in the transmitter that prevents the RF power amplifier from being *overdriven*. To understand why this matters, we need the concept of *linearity*.

An RF power amplifier amplifies a signal. If the amplifier is *linear*, the output is an exact scaled-up copy of the input — no new frequencies are created. If the input drives the amplifier too hard, the output *clips* (flattens at the peaks) — a non-linear operation. Clipping in the frequency domain produces new frequencies: *harmonics* and *intermodulation products* that appear as spurious signals on adjacent frequencies. In SSB operation, this is called "splatter" and it interferes with stations on nearby frequencies.

ALC prevents this by monitoring the output stage and feeding a control voltage back to the earlier driver stages. If the drive level starts to produce clipping, ALC reduces the gain of the driver stages, keeping the output just below the clipping threshold. The ALC meter on a transceiver deflects when ALC is actively reducing gain. For SSB, the ALC should deflect on voice peaks — if it is continuously pegged at maximum, the microphone gain or drive is too high and must be reduced.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A05: Why is automatic level control (ALC) used with an RF power amplifier?

- A) To balance the transmitter audio frequency response
- B) To reduce harmonic radiation
- **C) To prevent excessive drive**
- D) To increase overall efficiency
:::

### ALC with AFSK Digital Modes

**AFSK** (Audio Frequency Shift Keying) is a digital operating mode where a computer soundcard generates audio tones that are fed into the microphone jack of the transceiver. The transceiver transmits these tones as an SSB signal — the audio tones become the "voice" audio. The tones carry the digital data (e.g., for modes like FT8, JS8, or RTTY).

The critical difference from voice: the audio tones from the soundcard are at a *constant, steady level* — not dynamic like speech. ALC is designed for dynamic signals; it attacks slowly and recovers slowly. When it sees a constant-level tone, it drives the gain down as the tone continues, causing the transmitted power level to vary over time as ALC slowly compresses it. This level variation corrupts the digital encoding, which depends on precise audio frequency and level relationships.

Therefore, when using AFSK digital modes, ALC should be kept inactive or at minimum. Set the computer soundcard output level to a value that produces the desired power output without triggering ALC action. Monitor power output directly, not the ALC indicator.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A11: Why should the ALC system be inactive when transmitting AFSK data signals?

- A) ALC will invert the modulation of the AFSK mode
- **B) The ALC action distorts the signal**
- C) When using digital modes, too much ALC activity can cause the transmitter to overheat
- D) All these choices are correct
:::

### Vacuum Tube RF Power Amplifiers: TUNE and LOAD Controls

Higher-power amateur stations often use separate *vacuum tube linear amplifiers* to boost output power to the legal limit of 1,500 W. These amplifiers use a resonant *tank circuit* — an LC (inductor-capacitor) circuit — at the output to couple RF power from the vacuum tube's plate (anode) to the antenna feedline. The tank circuit has two adjustable controls:

**TUNE (plate tuning)**: This variable capacitor adjusts the tank circuit to *resonance* — the condition where the inductor and capacitor exchange energy at exactly the applied RF frequency, maximizing the voltage swing across the tank. Correctly tuning to resonance is indicated by a pronounced *dip* in the plate current (the DC current flowing through the tube). The dip occurs because at resonance, the tank presents maximum impedance to the plate, reducing current draw while maximizing RF voltage swing.

**LOAD (coupling)**: This control sets how strongly the output tank is coupled to the antenna/feedline. Increasing load coupling extracts more power from the tank into the antenna. The correct LOAD setting produces the desired output power at the rated (safe) plate current.

Correct tuning procedure: apply reduced RF drive, tune the TUNE capacitor for the plate current dip (resonance), then adjust LOAD for the desired output power at rated plate current, then re-optimize TUNE. This must be done methodically — a mistuned amplifier can destroy the vacuum tube or cause RF interference.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A04: What is the effect on plate current of the correct setting of a vacuum-tube RF power amplifier's TUNE control?

- A) A pronounced peak
- **B) A pronounced dip**
- C) No change will be observed
- D) A slow, rhythmic oscillation
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A08: What is the correct adjustment for the LOAD or COUPLING control of a vacuum tube RF power amplifier?

- A) Minimum SWR on the antenna
- B) Minimum plate current without exceeding maximum allowable grid current
- C) Highest plate voltage while minimizing grid current
- **D) Desired power output without exceeding maximum allowable plate current**
:::

### QSK Delay: Transmit-Receive Sequencing

When a transceiver is connected to an external amplifier, the amplifier must *switch* from receive mode to transmit mode before RF from the transceiver is applied. This switching takes a finite time — typically a few to tens of milliseconds, depending on the relay technology. If RF arrives before the amplifier relay has fully closed, the RF energy can arc across the switching contacts, damage the relay, or be routed to the wrong port.

The *QSK delay* (also called the transmit delay or sequencer) is a circuit that holds back the RF output from the transceiver for a preset interval after the keying line is activated. The sequence is: (1) keying line activates, (2) amplifier relay begins switching, (3) delay timer runs, (4) RF is enabled after the relay is confirmed closed. This protects the relay contacts and ensures clean, reliable transmit switching — especially important in CW QSK (full break-in) operation where the transceiver switches rapidly between transmit and receive.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A09: What is the purpose of delaying RF output after activating a transmitter's keying line to an external amplifier?

- A) To prevent key clicks on CW
- B) To prevent transient overmodulation
- **C) To allow time for the amplifier to switch the antenna between the transceiver and the amplifier output**
- D) To allow time for the amplifier power supply to reach operating level
:::

### Electronic Keyer

A **paddle** is a two-lever Morse code input device: squeezing one lever produces a continuous stream of dots; squeezing the other produces a continuous stream of dashes. An **electronic keyer** interfaces with the paddle and generates properly timed CW elements. It sets the element spacing ratios automatically (a dash is exactly 3× the length of a dot; the space between elements is 1 dot length; etc.) and allows the operator to set speed in words-per-minute. Without an electronic keyer, an operator would need a straight key and would manually time each dot and dash — difficult at high speeds.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A10: What is the function of an electronic keyer?

- A) Automatic transmit/receive switching
- **B) Automatic generation of dots and dashes for CW operation**
- C) To allow time for switching the antenna from the receiver to the transmitter
- D) Computer interface for PSK and RTTY operation
:::

## Antenna Tuner — What It Does and Doesn't Do

### Impedance Matching Fundamentals

A transmitter's output stage is designed to deliver maximum power into a *specific load impedance* — almost universally 50 Ω (ohms) for amateur equipment. An *antenna system* (antenna + feedline) presents some impedance at the transmitter's output connector. If this is not 50 Ω, a *mismatch* exists, characterized by the **SWR** (Standing Wave Ratio). An SWR of 1:1 is a perfect match; SWR of 3:1 means significant mismatch; higher SWR means progressively worse mismatch.

When SWR is high, the transmitter's output amplifier sees a reactive (non-resistive) load. Many modern solid-state transceivers automatically reduce output power when SWR rises above about 2:1 or 3:1, to protect their output transistors from the stresses of operating into a reactive load.

### What an Antenna Tuner Actually Does

An **antenna tuner** (also called ATU, transmatch, or "tuner") is a variable impedance-matching network inserted between the transmitter and the feedline. It typically contains adjustable inductors and capacitors arranged in an L, T, or pi network topology.

The tuner adjusts the impedance *presented to the transmitter's output connector* to 50 Ω. From the transmitter's perspective, it is looking into a perfect 50 Ω load. The transmitter delivers its rated power happily.

However — and this is critical — **the antenna tuner does not change the physical antenna or reduce losses in the feedline**. If the antenna is severely mismatched to the coax feedline (high SWR on the coax), large currents and voltages circulate on the coax, and the coax's ohmic resistance dissipates a significant fraction of the power as heat. The tuner at the transmitter end of the coax makes the transmitter happy, but the coax between the tuner and the antenna still has elevated SWR and the associated losses. Power delivered *to the antenna* is reduced; the tuner simply transfers power *from the transmitter to the coax+antenna system* as efficiently as the transmitter can manage.

The correct interpretation of G4A06: an antenna tuner's purpose is to increase power *transfer from the transmitter into the feed line* — by presenting the transmitter with its design-load impedance so it doesn't back off power.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4A06: What is the purpose of an antenna tuner?

- A) Reduce the SWR in the feed line to the antenna
- B) Reduce the power dissipation in the feedline to the antenna
- **C) Increase power transfer from the transmitter to the feed line**
- D) All these choices are correct
:::

## Test Equipment

### Oscilloscope

An **oscilloscope** is an instrument that displays voltage as a function of time on a screen. The horizontal axis represents time; the vertical axis represents voltage. Internally, it contains amplifiers for both axes: a *horizontal channel amplifier* (time-base) and a *vertical channel amplifier* (signal input).

The oscilloscope's great advantage over a simple voltmeter is that it reveals *waveform shape* — not just amplitude. This makes it indispensable for:

- **CW keying waveform analysis**: the rise and fall times of the keyed RF envelope directly determine key-click interference. A CW signal whose envelope switches abruptly (near-instantaneous rise/fall) produces a broadband click in nearby receivers — a splash of RF energy across hundreds of kHz. A properly shaped keying waveform has smooth, rounded rise and fall transitions of 5–10 ms, which confines the spectral energy to the intended bandwidth. The oscilloscope makes these transitions visible. The signal connected to the vertical input when checking a transmitter's keying waveform is the **attenuated RF output** of the transmitter (via a voltage divider, not connected directly — the transmitter RF output is far too high voltage to connect directly to the oscilloscope).

- **Two-tone SSB linearity test**: Two equal-amplitude, non-harmonically-related audio tones (e.g., 700 Hz and 1900 Hz) are simultaneously applied to the microphone input. The transmitter should amplify these linearly — producing a signal that is the sum of two equal sine waves, which has a characteristic "two-bump" envelope shape. When viewed on an oscilloscope and the drive is correct, the envelope forms a "trapezoidal" pattern. If the amplifier is *overdriven* (non-linear), the peaks clip and flatten, which is visible on the oscilloscope as flat-topped waveforms. Clipping generates intermodulation distortion products (IMD), which create spurious signals on adjacent frequencies. The two-tone test thus measures *linearity* — the most important transmitter performance parameter for SSB.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Multimeter

A **multimeter** (or VOM — volt-ohm-milliammeter) measures voltage, resistance, and current. The most important characteristic for voltage measurements is *input impedance*: the resistance that the meter presents to the circuit being measured.

**Why high input impedance matters**: when a voltmeter is connected across a point in a circuit, it forms a parallel path for current. If the voltmeter's impedance is low, it draws significant current from the circuit, disturbing the voltage it's trying to measure — this is called *loading*. A high input impedance (typically 10 MΩ or higher for digital multimeters) draws negligible current, leaving the circuit undisturbed.

**Digital vs. analog multimeters**: digital multimeters offer higher precision (more decimal places), higher input impedance, and auto-ranging. Analog (needle-deflection) multimeters have a notable advantage in one scenario: *finding a maximum or minimum value* (e.g., adjusting a circuit for peak or null response). The continuously moving needle makes it easier to observe the direction of change and find the exact peak/null, compared to rapidly changing digital digits that are harder to interpret in real time.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4B05: Why do voltmeters have high input impedance?

- A) It improves the frequency response
- B) It allows for higher voltages to be safely measured
- C) It improves the resolution of the readings
- **D) It decreases the loading on circuits being measured**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4B06: What is an advantage of a digital multimeter as compared to an analog multimeter?

- A) Better for measuring computer circuits
- B) Less prone to overload
- **C) Higher precision**
- D) Faster response
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4B09: When is an analog multimeter preferred to a digital multimeter?

- A) When testing logic circuits
- B) When high precision is desired
- C) When measuring the frequency of an oscillator
- **D) When adjusting circuits for maximum or minimum values**
:::

### Directional Wattmeter

A **directional wattmeter** (or "SWR/power meter") is inserted in the feedline between the transmitter and antenna. It uses a *directional coupler* — a device that can independently sense power flowing in each direction on the transmission line. It measures:

- **Forward power**: power flowing from the transmitter toward the antenna (what you want to radiate)
- **Reflected power**: power flowing back from the antenna toward the transmitter (the fraction not accepted by the antenna due to mismatch)

The ratio of reflected to forward power (the *reflection coefficient*) directly yields the **SWR** (Standing Wave Ratio). The SWR can be computed from: SWR = (1 + |Γ|) / (1 − |Γ|), where |Γ| = √(P_reflected / P_forward). The directional wattmeter is the standard tool for measuring SWR and transmitted power in an amateur station.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4B10: Which of the following can be determined with a directional wattmeter?

- **A) Standing wave ratio**
- B) Antenna front-to-back ratio
- C) RF interference
- D) Radio wave propagation
:::

### Antenna Analyzer

An **antenna analyzer** is a specialized instrument that measures the *complex impedance* (both resistive and reactive components) at the antenna feedpoint or feedline, across a range of frequencies. It is essentially a miniature RF signal generator combined with an impedance measurement bridge and a display.

Key usage rules:

- The antenna analyzer must be connected directly to the antenna system (feedline + antenna), with the transmitter disconnected. Its measurements depend on injecting a small known signal and measuring the response — a connected transmitter would interfere catastrophically.
- Strong signals from nearby transmitters operating on the measured frequency can couple into the antenna under test and corrupt the impedance readings.
- An antenna analyzer can measure impedance of coaxial cable (to check for cable faults or electrical length), as well as antenna feedpoint impedance and resonant frequency.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4B11: Which of the following must be connected to an antenna analyzer when it is being used for SWR measurements?

- A) Receiver
- B) Transmitter
- **C) Antenna and feed line**
- D) All these choices are correct
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4B12: What effect can strong signals from nearby transmitters have on an antenna analyzer?

- A) Desensitization which can cause intermodulation products which interfere with impedance readings
- **B) Received power that interferes with SWR readings**
- C) Generation of harmonics which interfere with frequency readings
- D) All these choices are correct
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4B13: Which of the following can be measured with an antenna analyzer?

- A) Front-to-back ratio of an antenna
- B) Power output from a transmitter

:::

## Grounding, Bonding, and RFI

Grounding in an amateur station serves two distinct — and sometimes conflicting — purposes: *safety grounding* (protecting humans from electrical shock hazards) and *RF grounding* (providing a reference potential for RF circuits and completing antenna current paths). Both are essential, but they operate on different principles.

### Safety Ground

The **safety ground** is the green wire in standard AC mains wiring. It connects the chassis of every piece of equipment to the earth through the building's electrical panel. If a fault occurs inside the equipment (e.g., a wire contacts the chassis), fault current flows through the safety ground rather than through a person who touches the chassis. All metal enclosures of station equipment must be connected to this safety ground.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4C12: Why must all metal enclosures of station equipment be grounded?

- A) It prevents a blown fuse in the event of an internal short circuit
- B) It prevents signal overload
- C) It ensures that the neutral wire is grounded
- **D) It ensures that hazardous voltages cannot appear on the chassis**
:::

### RF Ground and Resonant Ground Problems

An **RF ground** is a low-impedance connection to earth at radio frequencies. For vertical antennas, the RF ground provides the return current path — the antenna is only half of the antenna system; the other half is the ground plane or radial system.

A seemingly straightforward ground wire can become a problem if its physical length happens to be an odd multiple of λ/4 (quarter-wavelength) at the operating frequency. At λ/4, a transmission line (or wire) terminated in a short circuit presents an *open circuit* at its other end — very high impedance, not low. A ground wire that is resonant at the operating frequency thus presents *high* impedance to RF at the equipment end, despite being connected to earth at the other end. High RF impedance means high RF *voltage* at the equipment end — the exact opposite of the intended effect.

This "resonant ground connection" problem causes elevated RF voltages on equipment enclosures, which can produce RF burns (burns from touching a surface at high RF voltage) and RF interference. The ground wire being of high impedance on that frequency is the proximate cause.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4C05: What is a possible cause of high voltages that produce RF burns?

- A) Flat braid rather than round wire has been used for the ground wire
- B) Insulated wire has been used for the ground wire
- C) The ground rod is resonant
- **D) The ground wire has high impedance on that frequency**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4C06: What is a possible effect of a resonant ground connection?

- A) Overheating of ground straps
- B) Corrosion of the ground rod
- **C) High RF voltages on the enclosures of station equipment**
- D) A ground loop
:::

### Ground Loops

A **ground loop** occurs when multiple pieces of equipment are connected together through two or more paths that form a closed loop — typically through both audio cable shields (which act as a signal ground conductor) and through the building's AC safety ground. If any voltage difference exists between the ground potentials at different points in the loop (even millivolts, from magnetic induction or ground current from other devices), this voltage drives a current through the loop. This loop current appears as an unwanted signal in the audio — typically a low-frequency hum at 60 Hz (the AC power frequency) or harmonics thereof.

The solution is *star grounding*: all equipment grounds run to a single common point, so no loops can form. Bonding all equipment enclosures together at one point achieves this.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4C09: How can the effects of ground loops be minimized?

- A) Connect all ground conductors in series
- B) Connect the AC neutral conductor to the ground wire
- C) Avoid using lock washers and star washers when making ground connections
- **D) Bond equipment enclosures together**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4C10: What could be a symptom caused by a ground loop in your station's audio connections?

- **A) You receive reports of "hum" on your station's transmitted signal**
- B) The SWR reading for one or more antennas is suddenly very high
- C) An item of station equipment starts to draw excessive amounts of current
- D) You receive reports of harmonic interference from your station
:::

### Lightning Protection: No Soldered Joints

Lightning protection ground connections must use mechanical fasteners (bolts, clamps, compression fittings) — never soldered joints. The reason is simple: solder melts at approximately 183°C (for standard 60/40 tin-lead solder). The current in a lightning strike can reach tens of thousands of amperes. Even momentarily, this produces intense heating that vaporizes solder, destroying the joint. A protection ground that opens at the instant of a lightning strike provides no protection. Mechanical connections withstand the thermal shock.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## G4C07: Why should soldered joints not be used in lightning protection ground connections?

- **A) A soldered joint will likely be destroyed by the heat of a lightning strike**

### RF Interference to Audio Circuits

RF energy can couple into audio circuits through two paths: conduction (along wiring) and radiation (through space). Audio cables — even shielded ones — can carry RF as *common-mode current*: RF current that flows on the outside of the shield, not as differential signal between center conductor and shield. This common-mode RF current can enter audio amplifier circuits and, because audio circuits contain semiconductor junctions (diodes and transistors), the RF is *rectified* (converted to DC or low-frequency AC), which then appears as interference in the audio.

A **ferrite choke** (a ferrite core wrapped around or threaded onto the cable) presents high impedance to common-mode RF current but low impedance to differential audio signals, effectively blocking the RF without affecting the audio.

**Interference sounds**:
- An SSB (voice) transmitter interfering with an audio device produces *distorted speech* — because SSB audio is speech that has been amplitude-modulated onto RF; when detected by the non-linear junctions in the audio circuit, the original speech reappears, distorted.
- A CW transmitter interfering with an audio device produces *on-and-off humming or clicking* — corresponding to the on-off keying of the CW signal.

**Wide-range interference**: arcing at a poor electrical connection (a corroded or loose joint that intermittently arcs) generates RF noise across an enormous frequency range, covering many bands simultaneously. This is the hallmark of arc-discharge noise sources.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### RF Hot Spots and Equipment Bonding

**RF hot spots** are locations in the station where RF voltages are elevated due to resonances in wiring, connections, or equipment cases. Any conducting structure that is approximately λ/4 or λ/2 at the operating frequency can develop standing-wave resonances with elevated voltages at certain points. Equipment enclosures, power cables, and audio cables can all be unintentional resonators.

**Bonding** all equipment enclosures together with short, low-inductance conductors establishes a common RF ground reference across all equipment and prevents any single enclosure from becoming an isolated resonator. It is the primary technique for minimizing RF hot spots.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

- D) Placing low-pass filters on all feed lines
:::

## Speech Processing and S Meters

### Speech Processor

The **speech processor** is a device — implemented in hardware or in DSP — that compresses the *dynamic range* of the transmitted voice audio. Dynamic range is the ratio of the loudest to the quietest parts of normal speech, which spans roughly 30–40 dB in conversational speaking. This means that on unprocessed peaks, the SSB transmitter reaches full PEP (Peak Envelope Power), but the average power is much lower — because most of the audio is at moderate levels, not the peak level.

The speech processor compresses this range: it raises the quieter passages toward the peak level and limits the peaks. The effect on the RF signal: *average power increases*, approaching PEP more consistently, without increasing the legal power limit (which is defined in terms of PEP, not average power). More average power means the receiver on the other end hears a stronger, more consistent signal — better intelligibility on marginal-signal paths.

Over-processing (too much compression) produces audible distortion, generates intermodulation products that splatter onto adjacent frequencies, and can actually *decrease* intelligibility despite the louder apparent level.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### S Meter and Signal Strength

The **S meter** (Signal Meter) is the received signal strength indicator on a transceiver. It is calibrated in **S units**. The key calibration facts:

- **1 S unit = 6 dB** of signal power change. A 6 dB power change corresponds to a factor of 4× in power (since dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁), so 6 dB → P₂/P₁ = 10^(6/10) ≈ 4).
- **S9** is a standard reference level, typically defined as 50 μV across 50 Ω at the antenna terminals.
- **"20 dB over S9"**: 20 dB above S9. Since 20 dB = 10 log₁₀(100), this means the signal is 100× stronger in power than S9.

Practical consequence: to raise the S meter reading at a distant receiver by *one* S unit, you must increase your transmitted power by 4× (since 1 S unit = 6 dB = 4× power). Going from 100 W to 400 W raises the S meter by one unit. This is why experienced operators often say "more antenna is better than more power" — a 6 dB antenna gain (which achieves the same 1 S unit improvement) is far easier and cheaper than quadrupling transmitter power.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### SSB Carrier Frequency and Band Edge Compliance

In SSB operation, the radio's dial (displayed frequency) shows the *suppressed carrier frequency* — the reference point from which the sideband signal is generated. The actual transmitted signal occupies a band of frequencies adjacent to this carrier:

- **USB (Upper Sideband)**: the signal occupies frequencies *above* the carrier frequency. A 3 kHz USB signal with carrier at 14.347 MHz occupies 14.347–14.350 MHz.
- **LSB (Lower Sideband)**: the signal occupies frequencies *below* the carrier frequency. A 3 kHz LSB signal with carrier at 7.178 MHz occupies 7.175–7.178 MHz.

**Band edge compliance** requires that the entire transmitted signal (not just the carrier frequency) remain within the allocated band:

- **LSB**: your carrier must be at least 3 kHz *above* the lower band edge, so the lower sideband (which extends downward from the carrier) stays within the band.
- **USB**: your carrier must be at least 3 kHz *below* the upper band edge, so the upper sideband (which extends upward from the carrier) stays within the band.

Setting your carrier right at the band edge and transmitting USB or LSB means part of your signal is out of band — an FCC violation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Mobile Operation and Alternative Power

### HF Mobile Antenna Challenges

A full quarter-wave antenna at 40 meters (7 MHz) would need to be about 10.7 meters (35 feet) tall — clearly impossible on a vehicle. Mobile HF antennas solve this by being physically shorter than resonant length and adding a *loading coil* (an inductor) in series to compensate for the missing electrical length. The loading coil increases the antenna's reactance to bring it to resonance at the desired frequency.

The fundamental tradeoff: a shorter-than-resonant antenna has a very narrow *bandwidth* (the range of frequencies over which it presents a reasonable impedance to the feedline) and reduced radiation efficiency. Physical antenna length trades off directly against bandwidth and efficiency.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Capacitance Hat and Corona Ball

**Capacitance hat**: a set of radial wires or a disk added at the top of a mobile antenna. Electrically, it adds capacitance to the top of the antenna, which partially compensates for the electrical shortening — reducing the inductance required from the loading coil. Less inductance needed means a more efficient loading coil (lower coil loss), which translates to better antenna efficiency. The capacitance hat electrically *lengthens* the short physical antenna, allowing a smaller loading coil for the same resonant frequency.

**Corona ball**: a smooth, polished metal sphere fitted at the very tip of the antenna. At the tip of a thin wire, electric field lines converge to an intense concentration, which can initiate *corona discharge* — ionization of the air at the tip, which generates RF noise and wastes power. The smooth spherical surface of the corona ball distributes the electric field over a larger area, reducing the peak field intensity below the corona discharge threshold. This is the same reason high-voltage transmission line hardware uses smooth rounded hardware rather than sharp bolts and corners.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

:::

### Mobile Power Connections

A 100 W HF transceiver draws approximately 20–25 A at 13.8 V. The vehicle's cigarette lighter / accessory socket is typically wired with light-gauge wire fused at 10–15 A, shared with other vehicle accessories, and routed through the vehicle's fuse panel — introducing resistance and noise. At 20+ A draw, this wiring is inadequate and may cause voltage drops that impair transceiver performance or create a fire risk.

The correct installation connects directly to the vehicle battery with dedicated, heavy-gauge wire (typically 10 AWG or larger), properly fused at both ends, as short as possible. This provides the full battery voltage with minimal resistance drop and avoids the noise that vehicle electronics inject onto the shared accessory bus.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Vehicle RFI Sources

Modern vehicles are extraordinarily noisy RF environments. The ignition system, fuel injectors (which switch high currents at high speed), anti-lock brake controllers, engine management computers, and the alternator's switching regulators all generate broadband RF interference. This noise couples into the HF transceiver through the antenna (particularly if the antenna is poorly located near noisy vehicle electronics), through the power supply wiring, or through ground differences. All vehicle systems can be interference sources.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Solar Power for Amateur Radio

**Photovoltaic (PV) cells** convert light to electrical energy via the photoelectric effect. Each silicon PV cell produces approximately **0.5 V** open-circuit when fully illuminated. This voltage is a property of the semiconductor material (the silicon band gap), not of cell size — a large cell and a small cell of the same material produce the same voltage; the large cell produces more *current*.

**Series-parallel cell configuration**: a practical solar panel combines cells in both series and parallel. Cells connected in *series* add their voltages (10 cells × 0.5 V = 5 V total). Cells connected in *parallel* add their currents. A typical 12 V battery-charging panel uses enough cells in series to produce ~17–21 V open-circuit (higher than 12 V is required to actually push current into a 12 V battery, especially as temperature increases), with multiple series strings in parallel to achieve the desired current.

**Series diode**: a diode connected between the solar panel output and the battery acts as a *check valve*. At night or in low light, the panel voltage drops below the battery voltage. Without a diode, the battery would discharge backward through the panel. The diode blocks this reverse current flow, protecting the battery from discharge through the panel.

**Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries**: these require a specific charge profile — maximum cell voltage, charge termination method, and float voltage all differ from lead-acid batteries. A standard lead-acid solar charge controller may overcharge LiFePO4 cells, causing venting, capacity loss, or fire. A LiFePO4-compatible charge controller is required.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
